I'm reading through the paper on the human complement C9 gene, noting it describes two mutations causing deficiency along with a revision of the gene structure. C9 is the final component forming the membrane attack complex, encoded on chromosome 5p, and its deficiency is typically linked to recurrent neisseria infections.

Studying a Swiss family with inherited C9 deficiency, I'm tracing how exon-specific PCR and direct sequencing revealed two distinct point mutations, each producing a premature TGA stop codon - one a C-to-A change in exon 2 and the other a C-to-T change in exon 4, segregating independently in relatives and fully accounting for the deficiency. I'm also noting that sequencing the exon-intron junctions led to revisions of the boundaries around exons 4-6 and 10-11, with no extra introns found in exons 6 or 10.

I'm now working through DNA marker studies using known C6, C7, and C9 polymorphisms, trying to confirm that the identified C9 mutations link to specific haplotypes, and weighing candidate phrases for how the complement C9 gene and C9 deficiency should be named and annotated in this context, including whether population-level statements about terminal complement deficiency and neisserial infection risk should be excluded as too general.

Looking at "recurrent neisseria infections," I'm weighing whether this counts as linked to a described patient's diagnosis or just a general population-level association statement, since it describes a broad category of infections caused by Neisseria species rather than a specific patient's condition. Since it reads as a generic class of disease rather than an individually identified case, I'm leaning toward labeling it as a Disease Class rather than a specific disease entity.

I'm also considering whether to include "recurrent" in the span, since it's a modifier describing frequency rather than naming a distinct condition, so I need to decide if it's necessary for the minimal correct annotation.

Moving to the next case, "inherited C9 deficiency" from the Swiss family description — the gene symbol C9 anchors this as a Specific Disease. I'm weighing whether "inherited" should be part of the span, similar to the ambiguity I saw with "inherited spinocerebellar ataxia," since it's unclear if that word expresses a more specific disease form or is just extraneous context.

I'm leaning toward including "inherited" since it functions as an etiologic modifier, which falls under the anchoring rule for modifiers describing the patient's condition. So I'll annotate "inherited C9 deficiency" as the full span.

Next, I'm checking "C9 deficiency" where it appears again in "to identify the genetic basis of C9 deficiency" — same gene anchor applies, making this another case-level Specific Disease mention.

Then I move to "As a cause of C9 deficiency" and "heterozygous C9 deficiency" in the family studies section — both anchored by the C9 gene symbol, so I'm annotating both as Specific Disease mentions, with the heterozygous modifier marking the carrier status.

For "complete deficiency of both the probands studied," there's no explicit gene anchor in this span, but it's clearly referring to C9 deficiency contextually, so I'm treating "deficiency" as the disease head anchored to the probands being described.

Without a clear diagnostic anchor, I'll exclude "complete deficiency of both the probands studied" — it's a judgment call but I'll be conservative. The other C9 deficiency mentions ("cause of C9 deficiency," "genetic basis of C9 deficiency," "inherited C9 deficiency" in the Swiss family description) are already counted as instances.

For the title's "mutations causing deficiency," the bare "deficiency" lacks a clear anchor so I'll leave it unannotated. Similarly, "deficiency of terminal complement components" refers to a general class of several components rather than a single defined biological entity, so this generic statement also stays excluded.

For "recurrent neisseria infections," I'm treating this as a Disease Class since it's a population-level statement rather than a case-specific one, which fits the organism-modified infection-type noun pattern. The other candidate spans like "membrane attack complex," "exon-specific PCR," "point mutations," and gene symbols C6/C7/C9 don't denote diseases, so none of those get annotated.
